headline: DRAM shortage will last another 10 years, Adata chairman says, dismissing AI bubble talk until 2040 or 2050
summary: Adata chairman Simon Chen predicts DRAM contract prices will climb 20-30% and NAND flash 35-40% in Q3, asserting memory and green power will be the two scarcest resources for a decade.
details: Adata chairman Simon Chen (Chen Li-bai) forecasts the global DRAM shortage will persist for another decade, dismissing current concerns about an AI bubble. His comments followed a slump in Taiwanese stocks after TSMC's record Q2 results, which fueled worries about overheated AI investment.

Chen projects DRAM contract prices to rise by another 20% to 30% in the third quarter, with NAND flash prices increasing by 35% to 40%. He stated that electricity, especially green power, and memory will be the world's two most scarce resources over the next ten years.

He rejected the idea that Meta and other cloud providers renting out spare compute capacity indicate overinvestment. Chen argued that AI applications will permeate business, government, and consumer markets, and that analysts underestimating long-term demand based on short-term capital spending are mistaken.

Beyond data centers, Chen highlighted the growing demand from edge devices such as robots, driverless vehicles, unmanned factories, smart homes, and low-Earth-orbit satellites, estimating this pool could reach tens of billions of units. He suggested revisiting the AI bubble discussion after 2030, possibly in 2040 or 2050.

Despite significant capacity expansions by memory makers like SK hynix, Nanya, and China's CXMT, Chen believes these efforts will not ease the market. He noted that major suppliers have learned from past downturns and will expand cautiously, avoiding the disorderly capacity races that previously crashed prices.

Additionally, Chinese manufacturers face constraints due to restricted access to semiconductor equipment and lengthy fab construction timelines. Based on these factors, Chen stated that current discussions about easing supply and demand lack solid foundation, expecting prices and module-maker profits to continue rising through the second half of the year.

Chen's predictions align with Adata's strategy, as the company had stockpiled over NT$30 billion in chip inventory by late February. Adata was among Taiwanese module makers who raised approximately $880 million to continue purchasing chips, meaning every quarter of rising contract prices increases the value of their existing holdings. DRAM contract prices have already surged by as much as 171% year over year since October.

headline_marked: [[AI models found real bugs]] in their own adversarial review system, passing only after three failures
headline: AI models found real bugs in their own adversarial review system, passing only after three failures
summary: An engineer wired OpenAI's Codex CLI into Claude Code as an adversarial reviewer with a convergence loop, then pointed it at its own implementation. The system failed review three times, with each failure revealing a real bug.
details: An engineer implemented a system where OpenAI's Codex CLI acted as an adversarial reviewer for Claude Code, using a convergence loop. The system was then tasked with reviewing its own implementation, designed to ensure code quality.

The initial review process revealed several critical bugs. Issues included a broken output capture that hid session IDs, incorrect pipeline exit codes, and a flawed convergence definition that could wave through incompletely fixed findings.

Codex also identified a Windows command line length limit issue when passing large arguments, suggesting a fix using stdin. All eight initial findings were triaged and confirmed as sound, leading to a revised proposal for the system.

The revised proposal, though initially complex, was distilled into a lean version with clear rules for the models to follow. The core concepts of a findings ledger and evidence manifests were simplified for practical use within the skill.

To confirm the upgrade was complete, the new "done-gate" feature was applied to the upgrade itself. The system failed Round 1 due to unfixed output handling in some recipes and an undefined variable in a new rule.

Round 2 also resulted in a FAIL, highlighting two more gaps. One significant finding was a broken example in the skill's original documentation, which was confirmed to be an invalid invocation after a local test.

After addressing these issues, the system finally passed the adversarial review in Round 3, demonstrating the effectiveness of the AI-driven bug detection process. The experience provided valuable insights into robust AI-assisted development.
